title: Stairs, balustrades and handrails: stable stance and safe layout
audience: Cleaners who clean stairwells, landings, balustrades and handrails in residential, commercial, strata and post-construction work.
learningOutcomes: Place warning signs on landings and keep the route clear for other people.
Clean a handrail or balustrade with both feet on the floor, without leaning over or reaching.
Keep equipment and cables off the stairs and to one side of the landing.
Wipe spills at once and dry the treads before leaving them.

instruction.heading: Why stairs need their own rules
instruction.body: Stairs combine three hazards: a fall from height, a slip on a wet tread, and an object that blocks someone's path. Most of the controls therefore concern where you stand, where your equipment sits, and how quickly you dry what you have wet. People who use the stairs may not see the section you are cleaning, so signs and a clear route matter as much as the cleaning itself.

instruction.heading: Signs and the route
instruction.body: Place a warning sign on every landing you are working on, and at any point where a person could reach the stair you are cleaning. Keep the route clear. If someone needs to pass, stop, step aside to a safe position, and let them through before you continue. Do not cross a stair that is still wet while you are carrying equipment.

instruction.heading: Your stance and reach on the rail
instruction.body: When you clean a handrail or balustrade, both feet stay planted on the floor for the whole task. Leaning over the rail and reaching past your comfortable range are both ruled out. Move your position along the stair instead, so that each section comes within reach from a stable place. If a section cannot be reached safely from the floor, stop and tell the supervisor, who will decide on a safe method or access arrangement. Do not stand on a tread, the rail or any object to gain height.

instruction.heading: Equipment, buckets and cables
instruction.body: Keep all equipment to one side of the landing so that it does not obstruct anyone. Never place a vacuum or a bucket on a stair tread, where it can be knocked over or tripped over. Keep electrical cables clear of the treads and the handrail, where they can snag. If a cable must run near the stair, route it along the wall and secure it so that it cannot slide onto a step.

instruction.heading: Drying as you go
instruction.body: Leave every surface as dry as practicable. Wipe any water spill straight away, because a wet tread is one of the most likely causes of a fall on stairs. Use a drying cloth on each section after it is cleaned, and check the treads you have just finished before you move on. If a stair is still wet at the end of the task, the warning sign stays in place.

procedure: Place a warning sign on every landing you are working on, and at any point where a person could reach the stair.
Check the route is clear, and set equipment and buckets to one side of the landing, never on the stairs.
Route electrical cables along the wall, clear of the treads and the handrail.
Clean the handrail or balustrade with both feet on the ground, moving your position rather than leaning or stretching.
Wipe any spill at once, then dry the treads and landings as far as practicable before leaving them.
Leave the signs in place until the stair is completely dry, then remove them and store the equipment.

workedExamples.situation: You are cleaning a balustrade on a two-storey stairwell. A section is high, so you lean over the rail with one foot on the bottom tread to reach it.
workedExamples.reasoning: Both feet go back on the ground, and you do not lean over the rail or stand on a tread to reach. Move along the stair to a position within comfortable reach. If the upper section cannot be reached from the floor, stop and tell the supervisor so that a safe method can be chosen.

workedExamples.situation: A bucket is standing on the third step while you clean the handrail. A tenant comes down the stairs carrying a large box in both arms.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop, move the bucket to the side of the landing and out of the path, and let the tenant pass safely. Then resume the work from a stable position. A bucket on a step can tip, and the tenant cannot see it past the box.

workedExamples.situation: You have finished the stairs, but a puddle has formed on the bottom landing from the mop.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct action before you finish?
workedExamples.reasoning: Wipe the puddle at once, dry the landing as far as practicable, and keep the warning sign in place until the landing is dry. Do not leave the area until the surface is no longer slippery.

equipmentAndPpe: Safe access equipment only where the site procedure allows it, set up as the procedure directs
Non-slip footwear suited to the surface
Protective gloves for the cleaning product in use

commonErrors.error: Standing on a tread or leaning over the rail to reach a higher section.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep both feet on the ground, move along the stair, and escalate any section that cannot be reached.

commonErrors.error: Leaving a bucket or a vacuum on a step.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep equipment to one side of the landing, never on the stairs.

commonErrors.error: Leaving a wet tread without a drying wipe.
commonErrors.prevention: Wipe spills at once and dry the treads before you leave.

commonErrors.error: Removing the sign because the stair looks dry from the bottom.
commonErrors.prevention: Check that the whole stair is dry before the sign comes down.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Falls on stairs are a serious hazard. The controls in this lesson are the minimum set by the source procedure. The business must confirm its own duties before relying on this lesson.
Work at height, such as using ladders, scaffolds or elevated platforms, is outside this lesson. Refer any such work to the supervisor, who applies the business's height-work procedure.
This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate or authority for work at height. Completing it does not authorise anyone to work at height.

qualityStandard: Warning signs are in place on every landing being worked, and are removed only when the stair is dry.
Equipment and cables are kept off the treads and to one side of the landing.
The worker keeps both feet on the ground and does not lean or stand on a tread while cleaning the handrail.
No standing water remains on treads or landings at the end of the task.
documentationEvidence: Stair and landing checklist showing signs, the drying check and any section referred for a different method.
Incident record for any near miss or fall.
summary: Place signs on every landing and keep the route clear.
Keep both feet on the ground and move along the stair rather than leaning.
Keep equipment to one side of the landing, and run cables along the wall.
Wipe spills at once, and dry the treads before you leave.

knowledgeChecks.question: When you clean a handrail, where should your feet be?
options: Both feet on the ground, moving along the stair rather than leaning
On the rail, so that you can steady yourself while you wipe
On the lower tread, so that you can reach higher up the rail safely

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should a bucket or a vacuum be placed on a stairwell?
options: On the stair tread nearest the work
To one side of the landing, clear of the route
On the handrail, where it can be reached

knowledgeChecks.question: A tread is wet after you have cleaned the handrail. What is the right action?
options: Leave it to dry on its own and move on and do not mark it
Put a bucket on it to mark the spot for the next person
Wipe the spill at once and dry the treads before leaving
